title: Bidirectional BFS in Odessa: Meet-in-the-Middle!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS race across a street-map graph from start and goal simultaneously. The two frontiers expand level-by-level until they meet, cutting the search space dramatically.
ig_caption:
🌍🧭 Odessa street-map visualization with **Bidirectional BFS** ⚡

Instead of exploring from only one side, Bidirectional BFS runs **two BFS searches at once**: one from the start node and one from the target node. Each expands in **layers (equal distance)** like expanding ripples in a graph, and the moment the frontiers **intersect**, you can reconstruct the shortest path (in an unweighted graph) with far fewer visited nodes than classic BFS.

📌 In graph-theory terms: we treat intersections/road segments as a graph (nodes/edges), then search for the shortest route where all edges have uniform cost. This “meet-in-the-middle” strategy often reduces the effective branching explosion—especially in real-world maps where the graph is large but local structure is manageable.

🎬 Want to see how frontier size changes step-by-step? Comment **ODESSA** and share this reel with a friend learning pathfinding! 🚀💻
fb_caption:
Odessa (Primorsky District) in action: **Bidirectional BFS** finds the shortest route by launching BFS from both the start and the goal. When the two frontiers meet, you stitch the path together—an efficient graph search trick that can massively reduce explored nodes.
